**SiLU is a smooth, self-gated activation.** It multiplies an input by its sigmoid: $f(x)=x\sigma(x)$. For a large positive input, sigmoid is near one, so the output is close to x. For a large negative input, sigmoid is near zero, so the output approaches zero from below. Around zero, the transition is smooth rather than a sharp ReLU corner. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05202)

**Derive backward with the product rule.** Let $s=\sigma(x)$. Then $ds/dx=s(1-s)$, so $df/dx=s+xs(1-s)$. Given upstream gradient g, return $g[s+xs(1-s)]$. At x=0, s=0.5 and the derivative is 0.5, a useful hand-check.

**What a custom autograd function must remember.** Backward needs enough forward information to calculate that derivative. Saving x and recomputing sigmoid uses less saved state than retaining both x and s, at the cost of extra computation. Whether that tradeoff helps depends on fusion, memory pressure, and hardware; the educational implementation is not automatically faster than a library kernel.

**Distinguish correctness from performance.** Use double-precision `gradcheck` on negative, near-zero, and positive inputs, then compare forward/backward against PyTorch's SiLU. Testing only large positive values is weak because many incorrect formulas reduce approximately to derivative one there. If higher-order derivatives are required, test them explicitly: ordinary first-order backward agreement does not prove every autograd behavior is supported.

Keep tensor operations in backward connected to the graph when the intended API requires differentiability of the derivative. Avoid converting values to Python scalars or NumPy arrays, which would sever that relationship and can also force device synchronization.

**Technical details and references.**

SiLU is x·sigmoid(x), with derivative sigmoid(x)·[1+x·(1−sigmoid(x))]. Saving x and recomputing sigmoid in backward trades some computation for a smaller saved activation set. The custom function supports ordinary autograd and can be checked with double-precision gradcheck. A production fused kernel may make different memory/performance tradeoffs.

**Mathematical and practical explanation.** For $s=\sigma(x)$, $d(xs)/dx=s+x s(1-s)$. Multiplying this by upstream gradient supplies the custom backward. Double-precision finite-difference checks should include negative, near-zero, and positive values; testing only saturated regions can miss errors because both correct and incorrect gradients may be numerically small there. [3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.05202)

For the implementation or system context discussed above, see [1](https://letsdatascience.com/blog/activation-functions-relu-sigmoid-and-beyond) and [2](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/extending.html).
